daṇḍadhauti
(‘cleansing with a stick’)
------------------------------------------
Standard works on हठयोग like the Gheraṇḍa Saṁhitā give various cleansing processes, generally called ‘dhauti’, to purify the body and make it healthy and strong. It is only such a healthy body that is fit to practise other forms of योग like राजयोग.
The दण्डधौति is one such process and is one of three classed under हृद्-धौति. (See धौति">HṚDDHAUTI also.)
The योगि takes the plantain stalk or the stalk of a turmeric plant or cane and thrusts it slowly into the esophagus and then draws it out slowly. By this process the phlegm, bile and other impurities are expelled out of the mouth.
Like the other practices of हठयोग, this too should be practised under the direct guidance of an expert teacher, as otherwise, it may prove to be dangerous.

Daṇḍaka
------------------------------------------
Prince दण्डक, one of the sons of the famous king इक्ष्वाकु, is a fine example to show how a person can render even a fertile land into a desert, by his sinful behaviour. See DAṆḌAKĀRAṆYA for details.

daṇḍī
(‘one who holds a staff’)
------------------------------------------
Though, literally, the word means anyone who holds a दण्ड or a staff in his hand, it is a technical term used to indicate the saṁnyāsins or मोन्क्स्. The दण्ड or the staff which is a part and parcel of their monastic apparel is a constant reminder that the saṁnyāsin has to be ever vigilant to practise दम or self-control in all its aspects.
The daṇḍīs are of two types: the ekadaṇḍīs and the tridaṇḍīs. Whereas the former hold only one staff, the latter hold one, made of three sticks tied into one unit.
The single staff reminds its wearer that he has to keep his मिन्द् always under control and the three-in-one staff symbolises the control of the body, the speech and the मिन्द्.
See also SAṀNYĀSINS.

Daṇḍapāṇi
(‘one [who holds the] दण्ड or the staff in his hand’)
------------------------------------------
In the Hindu mythological and iconographical literature, this word can apply to यम (the god of death and the deity presiding over the southern quarter) and also to the god सुब्रह्मण्य (variously known as स्कन्द, कुमार and कार्त्तिकेय), more to the latter. He is shown as holding a long cudgel or staff (daṇḍa) in his right hand and the left hand resting on the left loin. He is also known as Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi, the meaning of this word too being the same.
See SUBRAHMAṆYA for details.

Daṇḍakāraṇya
(‘forest of दण्डक’)
------------------------------------------
According to the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि, the दण्डकारण्य is the forest where Śrī राम, the banished king of अयोध्या, spent most of his years of exile.
Daṇḍaka was one of the hundred princes, sons of the king इक्ष्वाकु, who had been assigned to rule over this area. His villainous nature made him molest Arajā, the daughter of his own गुरु, शुक्राचार्य. Consequently, he incurred the wrath of शुक्राचार्य who cursed him. As a result, दण्डक and his entire entourage was decimated and the kingdom itself reduced to a barren land, leaving a small part. Hence the name दण्डक or दण्डकारण्य to this region. It was also known—later on—as जनस्थान since several sages (jana = people) came there and settled down.
The area around the modern town of नासिक् (in Maharashtra) has now been identified as a part of दण्डकारण्य.

Daṇḍin
------------------------------------------
Sanskrit or सṁस्कृत is not only an ancient language but also very rich in its various aspects of grammar, poetics and literature. दण्डिन् (6th century A. D.) was one of the earliest writers on poetics. He probably lived in the Vidarbha region of Maharashtra. Three works are attributed to him: Kāvyādarśa (poetics), Daśa-kumāracarita (a collection of romantic tales) and Chandoviciti (prosody).
See also ALAṄKĀRAŚĀSTRA.

daṇḍa
(‘[that] by which punishment is [meted out];’ ‘[that] by which control [is exercised].’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘daṇḍa’ is one of the commonest terms that we come across in the धर्मशास्त्रस् and allied works. Etymologically, it means anything by which control is exercised, including punishment.
In its simplest form it means a stick or a rod. The stick that a Vedic student or an itinerant monk keeps constantly with him for protection in emergencies is a ‘daṇḍa’. It also acts as a symbol of self-control.
In the पुराणस्, it is the rod of death or punishment, in the hands of यम, the god of death. Consequently he is also called ‘daṇḍadhara’ or the wielder of the दण्ड.
A दण्ड can also be in the form of a long staff, a cudgel or a stick often unornamented, and is shown in the hands of some images like those of कार्त्तिकेय (or सुब्रह्मण्य), the minor deities such as मङ्गल, शुक्र and शनि (planet-deities), कपिल and even the goddess रति (wife of Kāmadeva or cupid).
As applied to a king it can mean the armed forces, one of the seven राज्याङ्गस् or constituents of a State. As one of the four ‘upāyas’ or means of achieving the desired end, especially while dealing with hostile kings, it means war, but as a last resort.
The word is sometimes used as a unit of time, an equivalent of ‘ghaṭikā,’ and is equal to 24 minutes.

daṇḍanīti
(‘[that which helps] to lead [people] by the power of punishment’)
------------------------------------------
Any civilised society needs a government and someone to head it and run it. In the ancient and medieval days, the king (called ‘rājā’) was the pivot of the governmental system. The science and art of governance was given several appellations, of which the words ‘rājadharma’ and ‘daṇḍanīti’ were most common.
The Arthaśāstra of कौटिल्य (300 B. C.) deals with the two subjects vārtā (economics) and दण्डनीति (statecraft) as one unit.
See ARTHAŚĀSTRA for details.
